proof_nl:
First note that D = r(b-a) is a nonnegative integer.

If a = b, then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a)/((q;q)_{r+a}(q;q)_a) = 1,
and D = 0. Hence q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = 1 = R_{a,b,r}(q). If R_{a,b,r}(q) lies in Z[q], we may take c_0 = 1, and the required symmetry is immediate.

It remains to treat the case a < b. From the definition of (q;q)_n,
(q;q)_{r+b} / (q;q)_{r+a} = product_{t=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^t) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)),
and
(q;q)_a / (q;q)_b = 1 / product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^i).
Therefore
R_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).

Evaluate at q^(-1). For each i,
(1 - q^(-(r+i))) / (1 - q^(-i)) = (-q^(-(r+i))(1 - q^(r+i))) / (-q^(-i)(1 - q^i)) = q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i).
Multiplying these identities for i = a+1, ..., b gives
R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = product_{i=a+1}^{b} q^(-r) (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-r(b-a)) product_{i=a+1}^{b} (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= q^(-D) R_{a,b,r}(q).
Multiplying by q^D yields the rational-function identity
q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q)
in Z(q).

Now assume additionally that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Since each factor 1 - q^m is a nonzero polynomial, the quotient defining R_{a,b,r}(q) is nonzero in Z(q); hence, when it lies in Z[q], it is a nonzero polynomial. Write
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j
with d_m != 0 and each d_j in Z.
The self-reciprocity identity gives
sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{m} d_j q^(D-j).
If some d_j with j > D were nonzero, then the right-hand side would contain the negative power q^(D-j). These exponents D-j are all distinct, so such a negative-power term could not cancel with any other term. But the left-hand side is an ordinary polynomial and has no negative powers. Therefore d_j = 0 for every j > D, so m <= D.

Now define integers c_0, ..., c_D by c_j = d_j for 0 <= j <= m and c_j = 0 for m < j <= D. Then
R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j.
Using again q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q), we get
sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^j = q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_j q^(D-j) = sum_{j=0}^{D} c_{D-j} q^j,
where the last equality is the reindexing j -> D-j. Since equal polynomials have equal coefficients, c_j = c_{D-j} for every 0 <= j <= D.

This proves both the rational-function identity and the palindromic coefficient statement.

domain_restrictions: a, b, and r are integers
q is treated as a formal indeterminate, not a specialized numeric value
n is a nonnegative integer in the q-Pochhammer definition
The product for (q;q)_0 is the empty product and equals 1
D is nonnegative because r is nonnegative and b minus a is nonnegative
The identity is an equality of rational functions over the integers, not a pointwise analytic statement
In the polynomial conclusion, R_{a,b,r}(q) is assumed to simplify to an element of the integer polynomial ring
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, the rational function R_{a,b,r}(q) is self-reciprocal of degree D = r times (b minus a), meaning q to the power D times R_{a,b,r} at q inverse equals R_{a,b,r}(q) in the rational function field over the integers. If this rational function is in fact an integer polynomial, then its coefficients can be indexed from 0 to D so that the coefficient list is palindromic: c_j equals c_{D-j} for every j.
quantifier_order: For all integers a, b, r satisfying 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0
For all nonnegative integers n, define the q-Pochhammer symbol by the finite product over j from 1 to n, with the n = 0 case equal to 1
Define R_{a,b,r}(q) from these factors and define D as r times (b minus a)
The identity q to the power D times R_{a,b,r} evaluated at q inverse equals R_{a,b,r}(q) holds in the rational function field over the integers

If R_{a,b,r}(q) lies in the polynomial ring over the integers, then there exist integers c_0 through c_D such that R_{a,b,r}(q) equals the sum of c_j q^j from j = 0 to D and the coefficients satisfy c_j = c_{D-j} for every j from 0 to D

witness_dependencies: The polynomial coefficients c_0 through c_D, when they exist, depend on the fixed parameters a, b, and r through the polynomial R_{a,b,r}(q)
The symmetry relation c_j = c_{D-j} uses the same coefficient list c_0 through c_D; there is no separate witness for each j
The integer D is determined uniquely by a, b, and r as r times (b minus a)

statement_nl: For integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, let q be an indeterminate, define (q;q)_n := product_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j) for n >= 0 with (q;q)_0 := 1, set R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b), and define D := r (b - a). Then the rational-function identity q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q) holds in Z(q). Consequently, whenever R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q], there exist integers c_0, ..., c_D such that R_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{j=0}^D c_j q^j and c_j = c_{D-j} for every j with 0 <= j <= D.

status_snapshot.last_transition_reason: The proof is correct and complete. It handles the empty-product case a = b separately, then for a < b rewrites the q-Pochhammer quotient as the stated finite product, checks factor-by-factor that substitution q -> q^(-1) contributes exactly a factor q^(-r) per term, and therefore derives q^D R_{a,b,r}(q^(-1)) = R_{a,b,r}(q) with D = r(b-a). Under the additional assumption R_{a,b,r}(q) in Z[q], it expands R as a polynomial, uses the self-reciprocity identity to rule out terms of degree > D by the appearance of uncancellable negative powers, pads coefficients to length D, and compares coefficients to obtain c_j = c_{D-j}. This matches the lemma sketch exactly and uses no undeclared or forbidden dependencies.
